#9407. Industry News: Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

📅 22 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1163 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident.
  • “I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada.
  • From there, it was a slippery slope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident. Already outdoorsy, he graduated from long hikes to planning to climb all 53 of Colorado’s 14,000’ers (mountains above 14,000 feet, or 4,267m). While researching which peaks required overnight camping, he realized that some people’s hikes just keep going.

“I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada. That’s just ridiculous,” Rice explained. “I fell in love with that idea.”.

From there, it was a slippery slope. First came the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), from the Mexican border in California to the Canadian border in British Columbia. Then he did the Continental Divide Trail (CDT), tracing the Rocky Mountains from Fresh Mexico to the Montana-Canada border. Before he knew it, he had a trail name — Iceman —and was working the gig economy to free up time for wilderness adventures.

But that’s where most people’s slippery slope levels out. Hiking the 4,988km CDT is as meaty a project as most of us can imagine. But for Rice, it only opened the floodgates. He was fascinated by everything that didn’t make it into famous routes, especially the ridges and mountains he passed in his home state of Colorado that were just off trail.

“There’s all this stuff the CDT doesn’t hit because it is following the Continental Divide,” he told ExplorersWeb. “So when I got to the end of the Colorado section, about 700 miles, I was thinking, man, if there were a 2,000-mile version of that, it would be my dream thru-hike. Just that non-stop, relentless brutality that is Colorado.”.

Colorado has 14,000′ peaks but also deserts. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Industry observers note that rice started thinking about a massive thru-hike loop of the state. His idea was to stitch together existing trails and form latest ones where necessary.

Sources indicate that “I dropped a load of pins across the areas in Colorado I wanted to visit, then I pulled out a public lands layer of the map to see how I might connect the areas,” he explained. “The three core design philosophies were beauty, breadth, and epicness. I wanted to see beautiful views, I wanted to cover as much of Colorado’s diversity as possible, and I wanted to take the most iconic and epic route possible.”.

In a recent development, unlike places like the UK, there is no “right to roam” in Colorado, so connecting the route to avoid private land was tricky. Occasionally, he had to link bits of public land and sections of trail in the “least worst way,” with short road walks when private property appeared to halt progress.

It has been revealed that as he tacked on mountain peaks and the national parks he wanted to explore, his route swelled to a monstrous 3,000km+. His itinerary now included all 11 of Colorado’s national forests, three of its national parks, 13 14,000’ers and 47 13,000’ers.

“This is not an efficient route,” Rice admits. “You could walk the full perimeter of Colorado and then hike the Colorado Trail [an existing 885km trail from Waterton Canyon near Denver to Durango], and then still have kilometers left over [to complete the loop].”.

According to recent reports, the Great Colorado Route. Photo: Donovan Rice.

According to recent reports, the route looked epic on paper, but Rice still needed to prove it could actually be thru-hiked. After months of planning, Rice set off on his Great Colorado Route from Gunnison National Park on May 14, 2026. He traveled ultra-light, carrying just six kilos of gear, with just a quilt instead of a sleeping bag and a tarp rather than a tent.

“I wanted it to be lightweight enough that I could be nimble on the mountains while doing these technical traverses,” noted Rice. Traveling light was wise. Rice’s Great Colorado Route is challenging, with plenty of scrambling and sustained time at altitude.

“The crux might be between Bailey and Rocky Mountain National Park. You go over the Mount Evans Wilderness, two 14,000’ers, hop on the Front Range across several 13,000’ers, and then across the Tenmile Range, and then the absolutely brutal Gore Range.”.

In a recent development, rice spent 141 days tramping his trail, eventually finishing on October 1 after 3,252km. While he describes the route as “definitely not beginner-friendly” — due to plenty of cross-country terrain, off-trail navigation, and route-finding — it doesn’t require mountaineering skills.

According to recent reports, “For me, the real sweet spot is Class three scrambling,” he says. “Once you get up to Class four, it starts getting really scary, and I had no tolerance at all for true Class five rock climbing.”.

However, he did pack an ice ax, micro-spikes, snow gaiters, and a lightweight helmet to protect against rockfall. He also made an effort to structure the route to provide relief between the most challenging sections, giving the trail an ebb and flow, and potential hikers time to decompress.

The Ballard to La Junta traverse. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Overall, his focus on scenic beauty over contrived difficulty helped keep the route somewhat accessible. This is notable because Rice hopes that other hikers will give it a go. He is building a website that maps the route, segment by segment, with GPS coordinates to help future hikers find the best places to camp or alternative paths depending on trail conditions. This is a May-through-October trail, but Rice stresses that it is unrealistic to expect perfect conditions for four and a half months.

Recent findings suggest that “This is one of those routes where bailouts will have to happen,” Rice explained. “You’ll have to take a low route or an alternate. I’m hoping to revisit some of the areas in the future and establish some of these alternative routes.”.

He aims to get all 29 segments of the initial route fully mapped on The Great Colorado website by the end of the year. It’s a significant project, almost as big as the hike itself.

Recent findings suggest that “I need to see how many people will actually give it a try. People can do segments. I’d love to see more thru-hikers do this, but the big challenge is that I think the majority of thru-hikers will look at this and think ‘that’s above my pay grade’.”.

Sources indicate that the Castles, Colorado. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Sources indicate that once he finishes the website, the level of interest might dictate his next steps. “I don’t know what level of formal recognition I want to try for. Do I want to try to get it codified? Or should it stay unofficial and remain just some cool thing someone did that published information on how to do it yourself.”.

Whether or not his Great Colorado Route ever gains the name recognition of the CDT or PCT, Rice has authored something unique, and in a world full of rehashes and copycats, that makes it special.

Rice looking down on Island Lake from Ulysses S. Grant Peak. Photo: Donovan Rice.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The federal funds rate is what banks charge each other on overnight loans, and the Fed’s target range for it is 3.75% to 4.00%.
  • The Fed’s rate-setting committee raised that range a quarter point on Sept.
  • For borrowers, the connection is the prime rate, which the biggest banks set 3 points above the top of the range.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The federal funds rate is what banks charge each other on overnight loans, and the Fed’s target range for it is 3.75% to 4.00%. You never pay it, but variable credit card and home equity line rates move with it, while the average savings account pays about a tenth of it. Check which of your rates are variable.

The Fed’s rate-setting committee raised that range a quarter point on Sept. 16, 2026, and left it there in its Oct. 28 statement, though two of its 12 voters wanted another increase. Its next decision is due Dec. 9.

For borrowers, the connection is the prime rate, which the biggest banks set 3 points above the top of the range. That puts prime at 7.00%. Most credit card rates are prime plus a margin the issuer adds, and a variable home equity line of credit (HELOC) usually charges a benchmark such as prime plus a margin. Each quarter-point move in the range shifts a prime-based rate a quarter point, on the date your account agreement sets.

In a recent development, other rates work differently. Your bank chooses what your savings account pays. The FDIC’s national average savings rate is 0.38%. A certificate of deposit keeps its rate until it matures unless its terms say otherwise. Mortgage rates have tracked the yield on 10-year Treasury notes more closely than the Fed’s rate for 20 years, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta notes.

The committee holds eight scheduled meetings a year and introduces each decision at 2 p.m. Eastern on a meeting’s second day. A newly introduced range takes effect the next day. The Fed’s meeting calendar lists the meetings after December’s, starting Jan. 26-27. When a decision comes out, check two things:.

Industry observers note that december’s meeting also brings the dot plot, a chart of each official’s projection for the rate. In the September dot plot, the median projection for the end of 2026 was a quarter point higher than now, an increase that would lift the prime rate to 7.25%.

  • “Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This morning, rescuers found the bodies of Japanese climbers Hidesuke Taneishi, 40, and Tetsu Hashimoto, 25, on Gangapurna West.

“Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times.

Hidesuke Taneishi (left) and Tetsu Hashimoto (right) with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure.

The climbers were attempting the first ascent of the 7,140m mountain and lost contact on October 15 at approximately 7,050m on their summit push.

In a recent development, A search-and-rescue team has been looking for the pair since October 19. Unfortunately, no one knew where they were on the mountain, or even if they were on the mountain at all. Therefore, the search started at Manang village, with no success.

Sources indicate that the team included helicopter pilot Sobit Gauchan, high-altitude photographer and climber Manish Maharjan, and IFMGA mountain guide Pansang Rinzee Sherpa. The helicopter dropped Maharjan and Rinzee at 5,750m, and from there they used a drone to search the upper slopes. They scouted the northeast and southwest sides of the mountain, and finally found the remains of the Japanese climbers’ higher camp. Today, they found the bodies on the south side.

As for the cause of the accident, Rinzee told ExplorersWeb that their observations of the terrain pointed to a snow slab collapse.

Several teams have attempted Gangapurna West, located next to the Annapurna massif in Manang district, since it opened to foreign teams in 2014. However, none have summited. The mountain is also known as Asapurna or Lachenal Peak.

Team leader Hidesuke Taneishi was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after his first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak, also in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hiroki Yamamoto.

Sources indicate that hidesuke Taneishi on the summit of Pholesobi Peak. Photo: Hiroki Yamamoto.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every year, the Banff Centre Mountain Film and Book Festival celebrates the best mountain and adventure writing, film, and photography.
  • According to recent reports, first, the two Special Jury Mentions.
  • Sources indicate that the Mountain Literature award went to Lone Wolf: Walking the Line Between Civilization and Wildness by Adam Weymouth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year, the Banff Centre Mountain Film and Book Festival celebrates the best mountain and adventure writing, film, and photography. The literary highlight of this alpine-themed celebration is the Banff Mountain Book Competition, with eight categories and one grand prize. The jury will award the grand prize at the festival, but the category winners have been announced.

According to recent reports, first, the two Special Jury Mentions. Jack Plant’s Spirit of the Great Bear showcases his spectacular photography of the Great Bear Forest. Meanwhile, Ian Nicholson’s Glacier Travel & Crevasse Rescue: Essential Skills for Snow Travel does exactly what it notes on the tin. “Of all the skill sets required for mountain climbing, perhaps none are as intimidating as glacier travel. But with carefully crafted instructions and illustrations, Nicholson takes us behind the curtain,” jury member Lauren DeLaunay Miller explains.

Sources indicate that the Mountain Literature award went to Lone Wolf: Walking the Line Between Civilization and Wildness by Adam Weymouth. Weymouth dives into the place of wild animals in modern Europe, a continent “undergoing profound climatic, environmental, and political changes.”.

In a recent development, black Bear: A Story of Siblinghood and Survival by Trina Moyles won the Environmental Literature category. “Black Bear seamlessly weaves together two complex storylines, laying bare Moyles’ relationships with her brother and with the wildlife she meets while working in a fire watch tower in Alberta.”.

Industry observers note that the Mountain Article prize, awarded to a magazine piece rather than a book, went to The Misfits by Chad Heddleston. Heddleston chose to profile rock climbing couple Jan and Herb Conn. “These two exist in the spirit and austerity of the pioneering European climbers of the early 20th century. The writing highlights their uniqueness and the integrity of their life choices,” jury member David Chambre remarked.

Pioneering rock climbers Jan and Herb Conn. Photo: Dwight Deal.

The Adventure Travel prize went to North to the Future: An Offline Adventure through the Changing Wilds of Alaska by Ben Weissenbach. “Weissenbach — an L.A. native with little prior wilderness experience — treks through the Alaskan tundra with a series of eccentric environmental scientists and returns with a fresh perspective on technology and a revitalized sense of wonder for the natural world.”.

According to recent reports, cabin Wild: Alpine Bivouac Huts by Ben Tibbetts won the Guidebook award. “A captivating volume that invites us to see the Alps in a new light, through an intimate journey around a selection of bivouac huts across Italy, Switzerland, and France,” according to jury member Rob Lovell.

The Mountain Image award went to Fjell: A Faithful Witness by Orsolya Haarberg. “A highly original book that takes us on a journey through the Norwegian highlands. It is as much an art book as a book about mountains,” explains jury member David Chambre.

Finally, The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland by Guy Robertson & Hamish Frost won the Climbing Literature prize. “The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland combines stunning photography and evocative essays in a truly spectacular ode to Scottish winter climbing. By profiling important routes through the eyes of the climbers who created them, Guy Robertson and Hamish Frost have created an exceptional book.”.

The category-winning authors get cash prizes and a chance to win the grand prize at the festival on November 5.

#9397. The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

📅 23 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1672 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks.
  • Industry observers note that in the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems.
  • Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks. Taken in 1909 and reproduced in books and journals, it demonstrated Muztagh Tower as a vertical blade, a slender tooth of rock and ice rising from the glaciers with no obvious weakness. Generations of climbers studied it and concluded that the mountain was impossible to summit.

Industry observers note that in the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems. But the photograph had misled them.

Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains. His uncle, Quintino Sella, had helped found the Club Alpino Italiano, and his father, Giuseppe Venanzio Sella, was a pioneer of early photography who published the first crucial Italian treatise on the subject.

Vittorio Sella combined serious alpinism with large-format photography. He made the first winter ascent of the Matterhorn in 1882, followed by the first winter traverse of Mont Blanc. Throughout his career, he carried heavy glass-plate cameras into the high Alps, the Caucasus, Alaska, the Ruwenzori, and the Karakoram.

Sella’s photographic technique was excellent. His plates were large, the detail exceptional, and the compositions carefully chosen. His work was much admired, including by American photographer Ansel Adams. In a 1946 article for the Sierra Club Bulletin, Adams paid tribute to Sella’s work, writing:.

In a recent development, “The purity of Sella’s interpretations move the spectator to a religious awe. Sella has brought to us not only the facts and forms of far-off splendours of the world, but the essence of experience which finds a spiritual response in the inner recesses of our mind and heart.”.

According to recent reports, vittorio Sella. Photo: Alpine Club Photo Library.

Sella’s most crucial Himalayan photographs came from the 1909 K2 expedition led by Luigi Amedeo, Duke of the Abruzzi.

Filippo De Filippi’s official account of the expedition, Karakoram and Western Himalaya 1909 (published in English in 1912), was illustrated throughout with Sella’s images. Those photographs remain among the finest early records of the range. One of them, a telephoto view of Muztagh Tower, became famous far beyond the expedition report, and inadvertently sparked a legendary mountaineering myth.

In a recent development, muztagh Tower (7,276m) is located in the Baltoro Muztagh of the Karakoram, on the border between Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan and China’s Xinjiang. It rises between the Baltoro and Sarpo Laggo Glaciers, just north of the main Baltoro corridor leading toward K2.

It has been revealed that the peak has two summits only a short distance apart. The eastern peak is the true summit, and the western summit is a few metres lower. From most angles, the mountain is a substantial massif with steep but not uniformly vertical faces. From one particular viewpoint it collapses into something that looks far more extreme.

It has been revealed that muztagh Tower taken from the Upper Baltoro Glacier in 1919 by Vittorio Sella. The tower appears as an impregnable tooth. The photo inspired mountaineers for decades. Photo: Vittorio Sella.

Sella took the image of Muztagh Tower from the upper Baltoro Glacier, looking northwest toward the mountain. The twin summits lined up almost perfectly. The long telephoto lens compressed the intervening ground and presented the peak as a narrow, knife-edged tower whose walls appeared to fall nearly vertically from summit to glacier.

It has been revealed that from other angles the peak revealed broader ridges and less precipitous slopes, but this single compressed view was the one that circulated widely. The effect was really dramatic, but as later climbers discovered, also misleading. In 1941, Sella’s photo of Muztagh Tower appeared in a mountaineering book under the caption “The Last Citadel.” The image fixed the mountain’s reputation for decades.

In a recent development, muztagh Tower, 1909. Photo: Vittorio Sella.

In 1956, a British team and a French team both set out for Muztagh Tower, drawn in large part by Sella’s photograph.

The British team, led by John Hartog and consisting of Joe Brown, Ian McNaught-Davis, Tom Patey, and liaison officer Captain Riaz Mohammad, chose the Northwest Ridge. They planned to approach via the Muztagh and Chagaran glaciers on the western side of the peak.

Industry observers note that the French party, led by Guido Magnone, included Andre Contamine, Paul Keller, Robert Paragot, Francois Florence, and liaison officer Ali Usman. They worked from the eastern side, aiming for what became the eastern arête after reconnaissance ruled out the North Ridge. The two groups operated independently on opposite flanks of the mountain.

The British established Base Camp on the Muztagh Glacier on May 28, 1956, at 4,282m. Through the first half of June, they placed camps on the Chagaran Glacier, avoiding the worst of the lower icefall by climbing the northern moraine and then threading seracs. Camp 3 was set on the west col at 6,355m after a steep ice wall. They reached the col on June 16, but took until the end of the month to move tents, fuel, and food up.

Recent findings suggest that from there the route followed the exposed crest of the West Ridge, a mixed line of rock, snow and ice that required fixed ropes on the steeper sections. Brown made a key traverse around a rock cliff on the South Face. Camp 4 was placed on the ridge itself at 6,439m.

Above the high camp, the climbing continued up a narrow couloir and then mixed ground. The final technical obstacle was a short rock leaf between the two summits, graded alpine V and exposed on both sides.

Recent findings suggest that on July 6, Brown and McNaught-Davis reached the western summit. The following day, Hartog and Patey, after supporting the first pair, crossed the connecting ridge and stood on the slightly higher eastern summit. Both pairs had to bivouac on the descent. Hartog suffered frostbitten toes. All four climbers reached the top.

Industry observers note that muztagh Tower. Photo: Hunza Adventure Tours.

The French established their Base Camp at 4,496m on June 12 after approaching from the Younghusband Glacier. Their reconnaissance swiftly highlighted the North Ridge was impossible, so they moved onto the eastern branch of the glacier.

They fixed ropes through an icefall and up a rock-and-ice spur, placing successive camps until Camp 4 stood at the foot of the summit pyramid at 6,300m. On July 6, as bad weather closed in, they spotted the British climbers moving on the upper heights.

Industry observers note that after the two-day storm cleared, the French regained the ridge, overcame two substantial rock towers, and bivouacked high on the mountain. On July 12, Magnone, Paragot, Contamine, and Keller reached the main summit through deep snow, six days after the British first topped out. After summiting, they descended to Camp 4 after dark. Dr. Florence had waited at high camp for more than 40 hours without radio contact during the summit push.

The British party therefore made the first ascent of Muztagh Tower. The French completed an independent second ascent six days later. Both teams discovered that the mountain, while technically demanding and exposed, offered viable lines. The route, while serious, proved less relentlessly steep than Sella’s photograph had suggested.

According to recent reports, the two expeditions were not engaged in a formal competition. They approached from opposite sides, followed separate routes, and maintained cordial relations. The British simply reached the summit first. The French, seeing the British already on top, continued their own line to completion.

Recent findings suggest that far from a bitter nationalistic race, the two teams demonstrated alpine solidarity. The French team chose the east side specifically to avoid interfering with British progress on the western side. Rather than abandoning their push in defeat after spotting the British on the summit, the French celebrated their colleagues’ historic achievement and resolutely pushed forward to fulfill their own objective. When Hartog suffered severe frostbite during his descent, the French team stepped in to provide vital assistance and support during the evacuation.

The southeast side of Muztagh Tower, showing the route. Photo: Guido Magnone for The Himalayan Journal.

It has been revealed that since 1956, Muztagh Tower has remained one of the least visited major peaks in the Karakoram. A British team in 1984 repeated the Northwest Ridge (Mal Duff, Tony Brindle, Jon Tinker, and Sandy Allan), though they reached the slightly lower west summit rather than the true east summit. In 1990, a Swedish party consisting of Göran Kropp and Rafael Jensen also successfully scaled the Northwest Ridge.

In August 2008, Slovenian alpinists Pavle Kozjek and Dejan Miskovic made a groundbreaking alpine-style push up the steep Northeast Face. They successfully reached the upper ridge crest, but ferocious winds ended their push. Tragically, just after beginning their descent, a ridge cornice collapsed, and Kozjek fell to his death.

The 2,000m Northeast Spur of Muztagh Tower showing the line “Think Twice.” Photo: American Alpine Journal.

Sources indicate that four years later, Russians Sergey Nilov, Dmitry Golovchenko, and Alexander Lange made the historic first ascent of the massive Northeast Spur. Their grueling 17-day climb via a fresh route named “Think Twice” reached the true summit, earning them the prestigious Piolets d’Or. The Russian team indicated in their expedition report that Muztagh Tower was 7,284m.

The 1956 French route has never been fully repeated to the main peak, and no further ascents of the true summit have been confirmed since the 2012 Russian expedition. Still, climbers continue to push limits here, most notably in 2019, with the first ascent of the Black Tooth (6,718m), a difficult lower spire on the mountain’s ridge.

Industry observers note that muztagh Tower (top left) and its Southeast Ridge, with a high point on the Black Tooth (6,719m). The solid line, with the two marked bivouac sites, is the line of ascent to Black Tooth followed by Simon Messner and Martin Sieberer in 2019. Photo: Simon Messner/American Alpine Journal.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This full-length adventure documentary follows kayaker Dane Jackson and a small team down Chile’s remote and wild Rio Cuervo.
  • Recent findings suggest that with an entire river to descend, the film wastes no time getting right into it.
  • According to recent reports, forty years ago, there was a road up to Lake Mayuin, the volcanic pool from with Rio Cuervo flows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This full-length adventure documentary follows kayaker Dane Jackson and a small team down Chile’s remote and wild Rio Cuervo.

Recent findings suggest that with an entire river to descend, the film wastes no time getting right into it. Dane Jackson rolls out into the complicated business of trip logistics, trying to find a way to get the team and their equipment to the beginning of the river. Besides him, the team consists of the trip’s mastermind, Kilian Astorga, and kayakers Tom Dolle, Eirik Hansen, Adrian Mattern, and David Sodomka.

According to recent reports, forty years ago, there was a road up to Lake Mayuin, the volcanic pool from with Rio Cuervo flows. It’s gone now, so they turn to helicopter transport. With their gear dangling below on a rope, the chopper carries them up into the mountain, depositing kayaks and kayakers alike on the lakeshore. They set up camp and settle in to begin the first descent of the Rio Cuervo.

The team scouts the head of the river, swelled with recent rainfall. Photo: Screenshot.

Recent findings suggest that the dense forest and sometimes steep banks add another layer of difficulty as they begin to make their way downstream. They have to proposal ahead, as there are stretches where it is impossible to bail if the rapids become too much. This means more portaging, which is painfully slow due to the thick vegetation.

When they do hit the rapids, on-board cameras capture the frenetic energy of whitewater kayaking. But the film makes no attempt to conceal the reality of a first descent. Much of their time is spent scouting ahead by drone, poring over satellite images, portaging, and standing about debating logistics.

Sunset arrives before the end of their portage. Camping in the jungle makes for an uncomfortable night. Photo: Screenshot.

Jackson and the rest of the crew soldier on, though, cracking nerdy jokes (the jungle is compared to both Dagobah and Fangorn Forest) and making the best of bad weather and rough camping. In the final few days, conditions improve, and they can spend more time on the water.

In a recent development, the contrast between their slow, grueling push forward and the wild speed on the river brings refreshing energy to the kayaking sections. When the river finally widens as they glide into the sea, it feels like a hard-won victory.

Running a 3.5km gorge. Photo: Screenshot.

According to recent reports, early in the production of a certain musical, Broadway director Harold Prince attempted to ask Andrew Lloyd Weber what the deeper political allegory or social commentary was behind the composer’s feline opus. Weber famously took a long pause and replied: “Hal, this is just about cats.”.

In a recent development, this movie is about kayaking. Many outdoor adventure films use the genre, and the adventure story, to explore grand themes, and some do so successfully. But when they fall flat, is it more annoying than I can begin to express. For that reason, I deeply respect the clarity of purpose evinced by Dan Jackson and First Descent Rio Cuervo.

Industry observers note that julia Clarke hikes beside a stream in Mull, Scotland. Photo: Julia Clarke.

Campaigners are demanding that the industry establish better and more accessible reporting systems, better safeguarding standards, and that operators vet their staff properly.

The Art of Progress: Climbing ethics are constantly evolving, and many are now reconsidering whether traditional ground-up ascents, minimal bolting, and preserving the original character of a route should take precedence over safety, accessibility, and the experience of future climbers.

Safe Deposit Boxes Are for Papers You Rarely Need – Not Your Will

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (411 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that put original papers that are hard to replace but rarely needed, like deeds and car titles, in a safe deposit box.
  • According to recent reports, the box also protects less than its name suggests, since the FDIC, the federal agency that insures bank deposits, lists “safe deposit boxes or their contents” among what its insurance doesn’t cover.
  • Getting into the box is the bigger problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that put original papers that are hard to replace but rarely needed, like deeds and car titles, in a safe deposit box. Keep anything someone may need fast or after you die, including your will and powers of attorney, at home in a fireproof safe or with your lawyer.

According to recent reports, the box also protects less than its name suggests, since the FDIC, the federal agency that insures bank deposits, lists “safe deposit boxes or their contents” among what its insurance doesn’t cover. To be paid for a theft or a fire at the bank, you need insurance of your own.

Getting into the box is the bigger problem. You can get to it only during branch hours, so a passport you need on a Sunday stays locked up until Monday.

According to recent reports, A death or a sudden illness makes that worse. State law decides who may open a box after its renter dies, and opening a box rented in one person’s name can require a court order or the bank’s own paperwork. Picture your original will and powers of attorney, the papers that let someone act for you, in a box only you can open. Your family then waits on the bank, or a court, at the moment they need those papers.

According to recent reports, store the papers in a fireproof safe at home, or leave the legal ones with the lawyer who drew them up, and keep copies in the box. Move the cash to a high-yield savings account, where deposit insurance covers it and it earns interest. And ask your insurance agent to cover the heirlooms under your homeowners or renters policy.

In a recent development, last, pick someone you trust to open the box when you can’t. Add them to the rental agreement as a co-renter, and ask the bank what your state requires before anyone else can open the box after you die.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Tech Report: Couple Cycle America's Upcoming Golden Gravel Trail

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (302 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Colorado couple Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle have cycled 6,124km along the newly opened Golden Gravel Trail.
  • The trail crosses eight states — Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, and Oregon — and stretches from Cape Girardeau on the banks of the Mississippi River to the small town of Port Orford on the edge of the Pacific Ocean.
  • Most of the route, roughly 70%, is unpaved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Colorado couple Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle have cycled 6,124km along the newly opened Golden Gravel Trail. The Adventure Cycling Association created the route this year to celebrate its 50th anniversary.

The trail crosses eight states — Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, and Oregon — and stretches from Cape Girardeau on the banks of the Mississippi River to the small town of Port Orford on the edge of the Pacific Ocean.

Most of the route, roughly 70%, is unpaved. It is the organization’s longest off-road cycling trail, 1,120km longer than the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route.

The Golden Gravel Trail route. Photo: The Adventure Cycling Association.

Stennes and Doyle finished in Cape Girardeau after 73 days, averaging an impressive 80km and around 12 hours of pedaling per day. “About 90% of it is mental,” they told Heartland News. “You might be tired, but you just keep on moving.”.

The couple are both experienced long-distance cyclists who have previously finished Montana’s Significant Sky Spectaculaire in six days and nine hours in 2022 (a self-supported 1,400km ultra-endurance race), among other bikepacking trips.

It has been revealed that jules Stennes and Patch Doyle during the 2022 Massive Sky Spectaculaire. Photo: Bikepacking.com.

It has been revealed that likewise, the Adventure Cycling Association suggests riders should be self-supported for the Golden Gravel Trail. Riders are advised to carry two or three days’ worth of food for the route’s most isolated sections, and up to a day’s worth of water. This is particularly key in the more arid sections, such as eastern Oregon. In Colorado, Utah, and Idaho, the trail traverses subranges of the Rockies and crosses the route’s highest point, Cumberland Pass at 3,668 m, in Colorado.

Stennes and Doyle say their journey included thunderstorms, aggressive farm dogs, and “countless hills.”.

#9382. Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

📅 16 Jan 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1483 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

📅 16 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.
  • “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers.
  • So, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

I thought to myself at the time,.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

So, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

Among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

With all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

Recent findings suggest that while my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the significant-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

Industry observers note that this level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

It has been revealed that as we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a newly introduced cost too since I was self-insured back then.

Sources indicate that my budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

This strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze proposal in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

In a recent development, but as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

In a recent development, when it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which claims that,.

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

Industry observers note that the only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I right now live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

According to recent reports, but I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Make the store brand your default on groceries. Across a typical cart it saves you a third or more over name brands, and on most staples it does the same job. Pay for the name only where you’ve tried both side by side and noticed a difference you care about.

Sources indicate that that third comes from price audits done for the Private Label Manufacturers Association, the store-brand makers’ trade group, on about 100 typical grocery and household items. The real question is what the store brand gives up, and on most of the cart it’s nothing you’d notice.

Simple staples are the safest switch. Flour, sugar, salt, spices, canned vegetables, milk, and eggs do the same job under either label, and so do paper goods, foil, plastic wrap, and basic cleaners. The same goes for store-brand medicine, as long as its active ingredient and dose match the name brand’s.

Recent findings suggest that most foods made from a recipe measure up, too. When Consumer Reports blind-tested 70 store-brand versions of foods like ketchup, peanut butter, and cereal, 76% tasted as good as the name brand. The rest are where a name brand can be worth its higher price.

According to recent reports, so buy the store brand by default, and pay for a name only after a cheap test. Get one package of each, try them side by side, and keep buying the name brand only where you notice a difference worth its price.

That test matters most for two kinds of buys. With cereal, coffee, snacks, and condiments, the question is whether you prefer a flavor or texture. With trash bags and dish detergent, performance varies, and a bag that splits or a soap you need more of costs more than it saves. Everything else goes in the cart as the store brand.

Sources indicate that compare by the unit price on the shelf tag, the cost per ounce or sheet, since package sizes often differ. A name brand on sale with a coupon can beat the store brand that week, so check the tag on each trip.

Say your staples, paper goods, and cleaners cost $100 a week at name-brand prices, and the store versions run a third less, in line with the audits. Switching them saves about $33 a week, or roughly $1,700 a year, while the name-brand coffee and cereal you’ve tested and prefer stay in your cart.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that set up your home filing system with a folder for each length of time you have to keep papers, from bills you can toss next month to records you keep for life. Sorting by how long a paper stays, not who sent it, means filing takes seconds and you always know what’s safe to shred.

The IRS states most tax records can go three years after you file, and a few after six or seven years. Records tied to property you own stay until three years after you file the return for the year you sell it.

Recent findings suggest that sell a house after 15 years for a profit bigger than what the home sale exclusion lets you keep tax-free, and receipts from a remodel in year two cut your tax bill. They add to your basis, what you paid for the home plus improvements, which comes off the sale price before the profit is taxed. Shredding everything older than three years would have destroyed them a decade before the sale.

Set up a file box or drawer with these folders.

Drop new papers in an inbox tray, and file or shred them once a week.

Sources indicate that scan what you can to save space, but hold on to originals of anything a copy can’t replace, like a car title and the permanent folder’s records. Social Security, for one, won’t accept a photocopy of the birth certificate you use to claim retirement benefits.

The week you file each spring, shred every past-years envelope whose time is up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A AAA membership pays off only if you’d use its tows, other roadside help, or discounts. Before you join or renew, look up what your club charges for Classic, Plus, and Premier. Then check the roadside help your car insurer, carmaker, or credit card may already give you, so you don’t pay twice.

AAA counts nearly 58 million members in the U.S., and its three tiers differ mostly in how far a tow can go before you pay for the extra miles.

Dues and towing limits vary by regional club. One Western club, AAA Mountain West Group, charges $64.99 a year for Classic, which covers a tow of up to 5 miles or to the nearest AAA-approved repair shop. Plus costs $99.99 and covers tows up to 100 miles, and Premier, at $124.99, adds one 200-mile tow a year per household. Every tier includes four service calls a year for each member and covers that member in any car they drive or ride in.

Recent findings suggest that then price the help you have or could add. GEICO’s Emergency Roadside Service, an add-on to its car insurance, starts at $14 a year per car. In most states it pays for the first 15 miles of a tow to the nearest qualified repair shop. Many Visa cards include Roadside Dispatch, which needs no membership but charges $79.95 for a standard call, with 5 miles of towing included. Hyundai’s warranty includes five years of roadside assistance on a newly introduced Hyundai, with no mileage cap.

In a recent development, say your older car needs two 40-mile tows a year on a long commute. Plus at Mountain West covers both for $99.99, while two calls to Roadside Dispatch would cost $159.90, about $60 more, before the tow firm charges for the 35 miles past the included 5 on each tow. The owner of a fresh Hyundai, meanwhile, would pay AAA for roadside help the car already includes.

Adding a household member to Plus at Mountain West costs $64.99 a year, against $99.99 for the primary member. Count AAA’s discounts as savings only on things you already buy.

Pull out your auto policy, your warranty booklet, and your card’s guide to benefits, and pay AAA only for the calls and towing miles they leave out.

#9369. Latest Update: 10 Cognitive Biases That Cost You Money – and a Habit to Beat Each One

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1459 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: 10 Cognitive Biases That Cost You Money – and a Habit to Beat Each One

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1459 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that cognitive biases, like anchoring on the first price you see, following the crowd, avoiding bad news, or sticking with defaults, steer your money decisions in ways you don’t notice.
  • In a recent development, try a quick test of anchoring first.
  • It has been revealed that in 2019, the world’s tallest living tree, a California coast redwood named Hyperion, measured about 380 feet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cognitive biases, like anchoring on the first price you see, following the crowd, avoiding bad news, or sticking with defaults, steer your money decisions in ways you don’t notice. Since you can’t count on catching one in the moment, counter each with a rule or a scheduled habit you set up before the decision comes.

In a recent development, try a quick test of anchoring first. Decide whether the world’s tallest tree is taller or shorter than 1,000 feet, then guess its height before you read on.

It has been revealed that in 2019, the world’s tallest living tree, a California coast redwood named Hyperion, measured about 380 feet. You knew the 1,000 was only part of the question, and it still set where your guess started. Each bias below shapes money decisions the same way, while every choice feels like your own.

Sources indicate that anchoring is letting the first number you see set your sense of what’s reasonable. A “was $199” tag makes $99 look like a bargain, though the $199 tells you nothing about what the item is worth or what other stores charge.

The fix is to set your price before you shop. Check what the item sells for at two or three other stores, decide what you’ll pay, and write the number down. Then judge the tag against your number, not the store’s.

The framing effect is reacting to the way a number is presented instead of to the number itself. A dealer who asks what monthly payment you want can lower it by stretching the loan over more months. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) claims a longer loan can mean smaller payments but more interest in total.

Say you borrow $30,000 at 7% interest. Stretching the loan from 48 months to 72 cuts the payment from about $718 to about $511, but adds about $2,340 in interest.

Industry observers note that to fix it, restate the number another way before you decide. Ask for the total you’ll repay over the life of the loan, not only the payment. Turn daily costs into yearly ones, too, since $5 a day is $1,825 a year.

The bandwagon effect is the pull to do something because so many other people are doing it. A stock or coin everyone seems to be buying feels safe because it’s popular. But all that buying helped push the price up, so a late buyer pays the higher price.

The fix is to write down why you’re buying before you invest, in a sentence or two, along with the price at which you’d sell. If the only reason you can write is that everyone else is buying, wait. Better yet, write your buying and selling rules down while you’re calm, and follow them.

Confirmation bias is noticing and believing the evidence that agrees with what you already think. Once you’ve settled on a car, a house, or a business idea, every good review reads like proof and every bad one like an exception.

The fix is to argue the other side before you commit. Write down what would change your mind, then go looking for it. Search the firm’s name along with the word “complaints,” and look up any bank, lender, or card company in the CFPB’s Consumer Complaint Database, which shows complaints about its financial products and how it responded.

Sources indicate that overconfidence is trusting your own judgment more than the facts support. In a budget, it means planning around what you think you spend instead of what you actually spend.

The fix is to check the record before you blueprint. Guess what you spent on food last month, restaurants and takeout included, then add it up from your bank and card statements. Build the budget on the statement total, not the guess.

Industry observers note that survivorship bias is judging by the success stories you can see, since the failures drop out of view. You hear about the friend whose side business took off, not about the people who tried the same thing and closed.

The fix is to look up the base rate, how often a move works out for everyone who tries it, before you copy a success. Of the business locations that opened in the 12 months through March 2021, 47% were still operating five years later, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports. Before you put savings into a business, decide how much you could lose without touching your emergency fund, and put in no more than that.

It has been revealed that the ostrich effect is avoiding information you expect to be bad, like a credit card statement you leave unopened. The interest keeps adding up whether you look or not, and a late payment can hurt your credit for years. The CFPB indicates one can stay on your credit report for up to seven years.

Recent findings suggest that the fix is to check your accounts on the same day every week, such as Sunday morning, so looking is a routine instead of a choice. Open every statement, check every balance, and pay or schedule whatever is due. If you still can’t make yourself look, a financial therapist or cognitive behavioral therapy can help with the thoughts behind the avoidance.

Recent findings suggest that status quo bias is sticking with what you have, or whatever was picked for you, because changing takes effort. Economists Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea studied a large firm that began enrolling new hires in its 401(k) automatically. Many of those hires kept both the contribution rate and the fund the initiative picked for them, a mix few earlier hires had chosen on their own.

The fix is to re-choose your defaults once a year, on a date you set, as if you were signing up today. Start with your 401(k), since the rate an automatic initiative picks is the same for every newly introduced hire, whatever their goals.

Sources indicate that present bias is giving today more weight than any later day. If you’d take $100 now over $110 next week, but would wait for $110 in 53 weeks rather than take $100 in 52, you’ve felt it. The wait is one week both times, and it only seems longer when it starts today.

The same pull lets a credit card balance carry over month after month and pushes retirement saving off to next year, since the cost of each comes later.

The fix is to decide once and let automation carry it out. Schedule a transfer to savings, or an extra debt payment, for the day your paycheck arrives, so the money moves before you can spend it.

Sources indicate that loss aversion is feeling a loss more sharply than a gain of the same size. It can push you to overpay to avoid small losses, as with a low insurance deductible. A deductible is the amount you pay on a claim before insurance covers the rest.

According to recent reports, say a car insurance policy with a $1,000 deductible costs $150 a year less than the same policy with a $500 deductible. Over 10 years, the $500 deductible costs $1,500 more in premiums and saves $500 on each claim, so it comes out ahead only if you’d file more than three claims in that time.

In a recent development, fix it by working out what the protection costs before you buy it. Weigh the extra premium against the deductible it saves and how often you’ve filed claims in the past, then raise your deductible as long as you could pay it from savings.

Sources indicate that selling brings out a related bias, the endowment effect, which makes your own things seem worth more than buyers will pay. Another, the sunk-cost fallacy, keeps you paying into something because of what you’ve already put in.

According to recent reports, put two entries on your calendar today. Make the first a weekly account check on the same day and time, and the second a yearly review of your defaults on a date you’ll remember, such as your birthday. Those two fixes counter the ostrich effect and status quo bias, which cost you money while you do nothing at all.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Search teams have found the body of Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, of Germany, who went missing after he reached Camp 3 on his way down from the summit. Evidence highlights he fell 1,700m to his death.

Recent findings suggest that waschiczek was one among over 200 climbers who lined up toward the summit of Ama Dablam this past weekend. He reached the top on October 25 with guide Sonam Sherpa, but for some reason the two of them stopped descending at a rather high point on the mountain.

“The pair decided to stay at Camp 3 overnight after borrowing a sleeping bag and other gear from other climbers,” his expedition outfitter, Real Himalaya Nepal, told The Tourism Times.

Recent findings suggest that climbers above Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Dorjee Gyalzen Sherpa.

Sources indicate that according to the outfitter, the climbers prepared to continue down this morning. Lama asked his client to stay in place while he returned the sleeping bag to the tent where he had borrowed it. When the Sherpa returned, Waschiczek was nowhere to be found, but his crampons were still there, which suggested a freak fall. A search helicopter was called, and the remains of the climber were found this afternoon at around 4,500m.

Waschiczek is the first fatality on Ama Dablam this season.

Together with Manaslu, Ama Dablam is the most popular fall mountain in Nepal. The latest enhancement from Nepal’s Department of Tourism on October 17 highlighted that over 300 foreign climbers had applied for a climbing permit. That day, the rope-fixing team opened the route to the top, and a massive summit wave started a couple of days later.

Industry observers note that virtually all foreign climbers are guided by one or two Sherpas, so the summit rates and numbers are remarkable. Local media estimate that over 200 climbers, among locals and foreigners, have topped out so far this season. Further teams should join them over the rest of October and November. However, no matter how tamed with ropes and anchors Ama Dablam gets, a fall from its steep slopes is usually lethal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Putting your tax bill on a credit card costs a processing fee of 1.75% to 1.85%, nearly all of what even a 2% cash back card returns. Pay the IRS by card only when the payment earns a sign-up bonus you’d otherwise miss, or a 0% intro rate lets you spread a bill you can’t pay at once.

Sources indicate that on a $5,000 tax bill, that fee comes to $87.50 to $92.50. A 1.5% cash back card earns back only $75, and even a 2% card’s $100 leaves you just $7.50 to $12.50 ahead.

In a recent development, the IRS’s card payment page lists two payment processors. Pay1040 charges 1.75% on a consumer credit card and ACI Payments 1.85%, each with a $2.50 minimum. An American Express card costs 2.89% at Pay1040, so pay with one through ACI Payments. Paying through tax software as you e-file costs 2.49% or more. A sign-up bonus or months of 0% interest can beat those fees by hundreds of dollars.

Industry observers note that say a latest card pays a $750 bonus after $6,000 in purchases, and you owe $6,000. Charge the bill and you pay $105 to $111 in fees and keep more than $600 of the bonus.

A card with a 0% intro APR, an opening stretch with no interest on purchases, lets you pay off the bill over months for nothing but the fee. An IRS payment plan charges interest and a monthly late-payment penalty until you finish, and most plans longer than 180 days carry a setup fee. Suppose you filed on time and need a year to pay $6,000. At the IRS’s late-2026 rates, a plan adds about $325 in interest and penalties, plus its setup fee, against $105 to $111 in fees on a card at 0% that long.

Pay the balance off in equal monthly amounts before the intro rate ends, since whatever’s left then is charged interest at the card’s regular APR. Skip the card in the months before you apply for a mortgage or car loan. A $6,000 balance on a $10,000 limit uses 60% of that limit, which can lower your credit score until the balance comes down.

In a recent development, IRS Direct Pay takes the payment from your bank account for free, and a debit card costs a flat $2.10 to $2.15. Before you charge the bill, multiply it by 1.85% and use the card only when its bonus or the IRS interest and penalties you’d avoid come to more.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu.
  • Sources indicate that manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the second time in just over a month, a violent storm is approaching Nepal and threatening two meters of fresh snow on already overloaded mountains. This newly introduced setback comes at the height of the trekking season and also affects several climbing teams, including those engaged in alpine-style expeditions in remote areas.

According to recent reports, the first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu. Worst of all, it caused an avalanche that killed 16 Base Camp staff on Himlung. The mountain remained open to commercial expeditions despite the accident, and several guided teams are currently launching their summit pushes.

Sources indicate that manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal. Photo: Shiddi Ghising.

Industry observers note that A low-pressure front that formed in the Bay of Bengal has now developed into a deep depression and will turn into a full cyclone tomorrow. It is expected to hit Nepal on Wednesday or Thursday through the end of the week.

In a recent development, the Nepal National Mountain Guides Association, in association with Senior Meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, has put out a detailed forecast. They note that clouds spreading out from this system will hit Nepal’s mountains on October 28, especially above 6,500-7,000m in the eastern part of Nepal, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. This will spread over the next two days, causing heavy rains throughout Nepal and snow at higher altitudes.

It has been revealed that authorities and local media have urged trekkers and climbers to modify their looks and avoid river areas and high passes. The main concern is for those at the moment in remote areas without InReach, Starlink, or satphones.

Trekkers should check with local agencies, especially those heading for the Annapurna and Manaslu regions. Several passes there were already cut or in poor condition after the previous storm and subsequent floods.

A Russian team in the Kangchenjunga region is acclimatizing to climb 7,710m Jannu. According to their latest report, they initiative to touch 7,000m before attempting their main goal.

Fellow Russians attempting the West Ridge of Everest have retreated to Kathmandu to rest and recover, so they should not be affected. Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov, all climbing without supplemental oxygen, are enduring some lung problems. They returned to Base Camp from their second foray up the mountain last Friday, without reaching 7,500m, as they’d hoped.

After climbing in the Cholu range, Jost Kobusch of Germany and his small team moved to the Manaslu area for the second stage of his acclimatization before attempting Everest solo in winter, also without oxygen and via the West Ridge. However, the poor state of the trails after the recent floods and the approaching cyclone have thwarted his prepares.

“The flood cut our planned path and, according to forecasts, the incoming cyclone will leave up to two meters of snow,” Kobusch told ExplorersWeb from Samagaon, where the team is pondering their options.

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, these days, topographic surveys typically show that a mountain’s altitude is decreasing due to shrinking snowcaps.
  • Industry observers note that mont Blanc is now 1.88 meters taller than it was three years ago, according to a recent report by France’s IGN (National Geographic Institute).
  • However, it may be wise to wait before changing the figure in climbing guides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, these days, topographic surveys typically show that a mountain’s altitude is decreasing due to shrinking snowcaps. But strangely, Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps, has grown significantly since its latest measurement in 2023.

Industry observers note that mont Blanc is now 1.88 meters taller than it was three years ago, according to a recent report by France’s IGN (National Geographic Institute). The upcoming official altitude is now 4,807.47 meters (15,772.5 feet) above sea level.

However, it may be wise to wait before changing the figure in climbing guides. Measurements are carried out every two years, and each time the registered altitude varies:.

Graphic showing the results of the last few measurements on Mont Blanc, by LaChangingMeteo.

Mont Blanc’s “summit is constantly shifting,” Jean des Garets, chief geometer in the Haute-Savoie department, told Le Monde. “Each individual measurement is not significant in itself.”.

So, what’s with the yearly differences? Obviously, it’s the variation in the thick but ever-changing snowcap that covers the summit.

Sources indicate that the mountain’s rocky summit measures around 4,792m above sea level. The snow cover varies with the seasons. The difference from the previous measurement demonstrates that 2023 was much drier at summit altitude.

Recent findings suggest that the survey team on itsir way to the summit of Mont Blanc.. Photo: ING.

Recent findings suggest that A team from the Order of Chartered Surveyors (Ordre des géomètres-experts) acclimatized first by climbing Bishorn (4,153m). They then spent some days measuring several points around the mountain. Finally, they climbed Mont Blanc via the normal route on September 15-16.

Once on top, they pinpointed the highest point using a GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) pole, which measures altitude in real time.

Recent findings suggest that the recent survey featured an interesting novelty. In addition to altitude, the survey also measured Mont Blanc’s gravity by installing a gravimeter on the summit for the first time ever. This measured the force with which the Earth attracts the device. In so doing, they wanted to determine whether the summit has sunk, regardless of ice cover.

Industry observers note that the gravimeter on the summit of Mont Blanc, September 16. Photo: ING France.

“When the height of Mont Blanc changes, we can’t know for sure whether the ground or the rock has moved or if the ice has melted,” explains Olivier Jamet.

It has been revealed that gravity provides the missing information: mass. If the ice has melted, there is less material under the instrument, but the rock has moved closer to it. Distinguishing these two effects requires a model of the ice cap and the massif, and above all, repeated measurements at the same location. And the effort is worthwhile, especially now that the effects of climate change on Alpine glaciers are becoming increasingly apparent.

The gravimeter on the top of Mont Blanc measured the gravity at 9.7944689 m/s².

Recent findings suggest that “For comparison, this value is 9.81 m/s² in Marseille (located at sea level) and 9.8043046 m/s² in Saint-Gervais-Le Fayet (580m above sea level),” ING reports. “This difference in value, even if it seems small, allows for the detection of changes in mass, particularly in the mass of the ice. Repeated over time, these gravity measurements will thus contribute to improving the determination of the altitude of the highest peak in Western Europe.”.

Industry News: 7 Utility Company Scams – Check Each One With the Number on Your Bill

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that utility scammers rush you to pay or share account details before you can check.
  • Recent findings suggest that utilities set out those two rules themselves, through the Edison Electric Institute and Utilities United Against Scams (UUAS), a group of more than 150 electric, water, and natural gas utilities.
  • Every scam below asks you to pay, or to hand something over, in a way your utility doesn’t.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that utility scammers rush you to pay or share account details before you can check. A real utility sends multiple notices before any shutoff and never asks for payment by gift card, prepaid debit card, or crypto. So hang up, shut the door, or skip the link, then call the number printed on your bill.

Recent findings suggest that utilities set out those two rules themselves, through the Edison Electric Institute and Utilities United Against Scams (UUAS), a group of more than 150 electric, water, and natural gas utilities. By November 2024, the group had helped shut down more than 14,830 toll-free numbers that scammers used against utility customers.

Every scam below asks you to pay, or to hand something over, in a way your utility doesn’t. Your utility already has your account number and payment history, so one call to the number printed on your bill tells you whether a phone call, visit, text, or ad came from it.

In states that let you buy electricity or gas from a tech giant other than your utility, some of those companies send salespeople door to door. Maryland’s attorney general has warned that they may wear badges that look like the utility’s, say the utility authorized them to review your bill or is changing how it bills, and then ask to see a copy.

That bill holds everything a supplier needs to switch you without your permission. Your utility already knows what’s on your bill, so anyone at the door who needs to see it isn’t from the utility.

It has been revealed that say no, and ask for written material you can read later, as the Illinois attorney general’s office advises. That office also notes that the supply section of your bill names the supplier you’re enrolled with. Check yours, and report a name you didn’t choose to your state’s utility commission or attorney general.

Industry observers note that A call, text, or email claims your bill is past due and your service will be cut off within the hour unless you pay right now. Caller ID may show your utility’s number, since scammers can fake it. Some send a payment link, or a QR code or barcode to pay at a store’s checkout or bill-pay kiosk, where the money goes straight to them.

Industry observers note that your utility mails disconnection notices before it cuts service, according to UUAS’s consumer guide to impostor scams, and a call, text, or visit is never its first and only warning. It also doesn’t tell you how you must pay. The Federal Trade Commission indicates only a scammer insists on a wire transfer, gift card, payment app, or crypto.

Recent findings suggest that hang up or delete the message without paying, and don’t call back any number the caller gives you. Check your balance through the number on your bill or your utility’s own app.

After a storm knocks out power, a caller claiming to be from your utility offers to move you up the repair list, or to reconnect you, for an upfront payment or a reconnection fee.

Utilities don’t charge to restore electricity, gas, or water service after an outage, the UUAS guide says, and any charge that does apply goes on your utility bill. If your own equipment needs repairs before power can come back, the utility will usually tell you to hire a licensed contractor.

Hang up, and follow restoration updates through your utility’s website, app, or the number on your bill.

According to recent reports, A caller, or someone at your door in a safety vest, says your meter or other equipment must be reset, repaired, or replaced and that you owe a fee for the work. Some threaten to come back and remove the meter if you don’t pay. Others claim there’s a gas or water leak nearby and ask to come inside, while a partner slips in to steal.

Sources indicate that A vest, a hard hat, and a badge prove nothing, since the UUAS guide notes they’re easy to buy online or print at home. A utility that needs to replace equipment contacts you ahead of time and doesn’t collect a separate payment for the work. A worker who needs to come inside will have an appointment and photo ID.

Keep the door locked, ask for ID through it, and call the number on your bill to confirm the visit before anyone comes in.

A robocall or caller says you overpaid your bill and promises a cash refund, sometimes with a discount on future bills, once you press a number or read off your bank account or card number.

Utility companies don’t usually give cash refunds, the FTC notes, and credit the extra to your account instead. The UUAS guide adds that some mail a check to the address on file. A caller who needs your bank or card number to send a refund is running the scam. At best, the FTC states, the call is a sales pitch from another energy provider, which could leave you paying two bills, your utility’s and the upcoming provider’s.

Hang up without pressing anything, then check for a credit in your online account or at the number on your bill.

The payment can seem to go through for a day or more, since a bank can take that long to reject it, but no money ever reaches the utility. The bill stays due, your utility may add a returned-payment fee, and the scammer keeps your Social Security number for identity theft.

The real federal help with energy bills doesn’t work this way. The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) pays no grants directly to individuals and charges no fee, according to the Department of Health and Human Services. States, tribes, and territories run it, and you apply through a local office. The department asks you to report any message offering a LIHEAP grant or asking for a fee to its fraud hotline, 1-800-447-8477.

A caller posing as a federal agency is a government impostor, and the FTC says a real agency won’t call, text, or email you for money or personal information. If you’re behind on a bill, call the number on yours and ask about payment prepares and assistance, LIHEAP included.

Recent findings suggest that messages made to look like your utility’s, down to the logo, link to pages that ask for your login, card number, or a payment. Search ads work the same way, with sponsored results at the top of the page that lead to fake bill-payment sites.

In a recent development, utilities typically don’t text you unless you signed up for their alerts, the UUAS guide says. Assume any link, attachment, or QR code you didn’t ask for came from a scammer until your utility confirms it.

Type the web address printed on your bill, or open your utility’s own app, and never pay a bill through a search ad.

Sources indicate that call the number on your bill to report every attempt, even one you stopped. Tell your utility the name the scammer used, the number they called from or gave you, and how they wanted to be paid. Customer reports helped UUAS shut down those 14,830 numbers.

According to recent reports, if you already paid, call the gift card issuer, your bank, or the payment app right away and ask for your money back. Hold on to any gift card and its receipt.

Then report the scam to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, whether or not you lost money.
