Sources indicate that from its humble beginnings in 2008 to today, Bitcoin’s history has been relatively short but very eventful. The original protocol for this popular digital currency was created in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, believed to be a pseudonym for an unknown developer or group of developers.

Nakamoto launched the Bitcoin network just a year later and began mining the currency— an estimated 1 million bitcoins were mined in the early years.

The creator(s) of this first-of-its-kind asset developed the cryptocurrency in response to the Great Recession of 2007-2009, spurred by a distrust of the traditional banking system and concerns about its stability.

Given the recent values of Bitcoin, it’s hard to believe the currency first started trading on exchanges in 2010 at under $0.10. Since then, it’s experienced astronomical growth and some pretty wild price swings.

At its most recent high, one bitcoin was worth over $64,000—a far cry from trading for pennies in its earliest days.

In a recent development, whether you’re thinking of investing in Bitcoin or you’ve held this cryptocurrency for several years, it’s fun to look back at this groundbreaking asset’s history. Read on for insights on Bitcoin milestones, historical returns, and how its returns compare to those of other assets.

Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

📅 25 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.
  • Industry observers note that the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years.
  • Recent findings suggest that this means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

Industry observers note that the value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

Recent findings suggest that this means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

Industry observers note that is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:.

Recent findings suggest that “The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”.

To answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:.

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

If the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

Your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

Now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment).

But in that same time period, your share of organization earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com.

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

So as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

Industry observers note that that doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

Industry observers note that but Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a big Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

Industry observers note that this is exactly why the price of an individual company’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

But what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more swiftly?

In the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 major companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

These are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45).

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

Sources indicate that there’s one common theme in the big tech organization boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

But that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a new era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

Recent findings suggest that they may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

Having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

According to recent reports, but the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

It has been revealed that while the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

It has been revealed that so What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

As I said earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:.

Our economy will continue to grow and tech giant earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies.

Sources indicate that everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

Sources indicate that for starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:.

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:.

According to recent reports, wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

Recent findings suggest that just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

So far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

Sources indicate that it’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

What About Paying Off Your House?

Recent findings suggest that over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

If you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

Sources indicate that then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

In the Comments: what are your thoughts on the current stock market boom, future crashes and busts, and the role of Artificial Intelligence in our future?

It has been revealed that best Buy, Staples, Home Depot, and Lowe’s still match a competitor’s lower price, while Target and Walmart now match only their own. Nearly all refuse a third-party seller’s price or a Black Friday deal, so read the store’s policy and pull up the listing on your phone before you pay.

Recent findings suggest that best Buy and Staples both match a lower Amazon price, but only on items Amazon sells and ships itself, not ones from the independent third-party sellers on its site. Neither honors a rival’s Black Friday deal, and Best Buy refuses any rival’s price from the Thursday before Thanksgiving through the Monday after.

Each store sets its own exclusions, and the policies differ again after checkout, since only some refund the difference when the store’s own price drops.

In a recent development, all six require the identical item, so compare the model number and color before you ask. On a price comparison site, also check who sells each listing, since a third-party seller’s price won’t count.

Best Buy’s list of qualified competitors names 19 retailers, among them Amazon, Apple, Walmart, Target, and Home Depot. The item must be new, sold by Best Buy, and ready to ship or pick up from the rival right away, and clearance, open-box, and refurbished items don’t qualify. Neither does a rival’s daily or hourly sale.

Industry observers note that in a store, show an employee the rival’s ad or web page with the lower price still in effect. For a BestBuy.com order, use Best Buy’s online chat or call 1-888-237-8289.

It has been revealed that after you buy, only Best Buy’s own lower price counts, and only through your return window, which is 15 days for most shoppers and 60 for members of its My Best Buy Plus and Total programs. This season, most items bought from Oct. 30 through Dec. 31 can be matched to a lower Best Buy price through Jan. 15.

According to recent reports, beyond Amazon, Staples matches any retailer that sells under the same brand both in stores and online. The match works only when you buy in a Staples store, so bring proof of the lower price to the customer service desk.

The item must be fresh, identical down to the model number, and in stock at the rival. Clearance, limited-time sales, Cyber Monday deals, and in-store pickup orders don’t qualify. If a Staples store or Staples.com lowers its price within 14 days of your purchase, show the lower price and Staples refunds the difference.

According to recent reports, home Depot’s price match guarantee covers stores in your area and online rivals including Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Lowe’s, and Menards, as long as the rival can deliver to you. It won’t match third-party sellers or membership and auction sites such as Costco, Sam’s Club, and eBay, and it skips clearance items and Black Friday or other limited-time promotions.

Show the cashier the ad, printout, or web page at checkout, or use live chat or call 1-800-430-3376 for a homedepot.com order. Within 30 days of purchase, Home Depot will also refund the difference when its own price or a matched rival’s drops, though not on clearance items or anything bought during a promotional event.

In a recent development, lowe’s Lowest Price Guarantee matches a lower price on the identical in-stock item at another local store, or at an online retailer that ships to you, with shipping or delivery added to the rival’s price. On Amazon, it matches only what Amazon sells itself, and it skips membership warehouse clubs, third-party sellers, clearance, and one-time promotions such as Black Friday. Its stores also won’t match a lower Lowes.com price.

According to recent reports, in a store, show an associate the ad, web page, printout, or photo. For a lower price at an online retailer, chat with Lowe’s or call 1-877-465-6937. The policy notes nothing about refunding a price that drops after you buy, so get the match before you pay.

According to recent reports, target’s price match guarantee covers only Target’s own prices, so a lower price at Amazon or Walmart doesn’t count. It matches a lower price at Target.com, in Target stores, or through a Target Circle member deal, at checkout or within 14 days after you buy. This season, an item bought from Nov. 1 can be matched to a lower Target price through Dec. 24.

According to recent reports, A store purchase can’t be matched to a different Target store’s price, and clearance, closeout, and open-package items are excluded. Show the online price or digital ad on your phone, since the lower price must still be posted when you ask. Bring your receipt to Guest Services, or chat online or call 1-800-591-3869 for an online order.

It has been revealed that walmart’s price match policy works only in its stores. A store will match the identical item’s lower price on Walmart.com if it’s in stock online when you ask, but Walmart.com itself matches nothing, and neither one matches another retailer.

It has been revealed that after checkout, four of the six still refund the difference when the price drops, though each waits for you to ask. Home Depot allows 30 days and also counts a matched rival’s lower price. Best Buy matches its own lower price through your return window, and Target and Staples match theirs for 14 days. Best Buy and Target both stretch those windows for holiday buys. The Walmart and Lowe’s policies promise nothing after you pay.

Mark the window’s last day on your calendar at checkout, recheck the price on the store’s own site a few days before it, and ask for a price adjustment the day you see a drop.

  • Sources indicate that when he left Newly introduced Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, Robert Cowden, 52, set off on foot from Fresh Haven, Kansas, on a two-stage journey across the United States. First, he planned to walk nearly 2,000km to Pittsburgh, then canoe 3,200km downriver to the Gulf of Mexico. With him is his dog, Enzo, a pointer-mix.

Recent findings suggest that robert Cowden and Enzo. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition.

Sources indicate that when he left Newly introduced Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point. His battle with alcohol addiction had cost him his job, car, and home. Entering a residential treatment program would leave Enzo with no place to go. Now sober and with housing waiting for him after the end of his journey, Cowden sees his expedition as part of the larger effort to rebuild his life.

In a recent development, during the walking stage, Cowden towed his camping gear and supplies in a cart, which Enzo could ride in to take a break from walking. Setting out with very little, Cowden has relied on the kindness of strangers, both online and on the trail, to continue his expedition.

According to recent reports, “The number one warning you’re going to get on a walk across America is, ‘Be careful, there’s creepy people and bad people,'” Cowden recalled, speaking to a local KOMU 8 reporter while passing through Missouri. Instead, he’s been overwhelmingly met with generosity and helpfulness.

Cowden shows the wear on his trail shoes, as Enzo looks on. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition.

Cowden completed the walking stage in September. Now, he’s on the Ohio River and hopes to reach the Gulf by the end of 2026. While the second stage lets him and Enzo get off their feet, it has its own challenges. They released the canoe into the Allegheny River at Pittsburgh. It soon joined the Ohio, and lengthy stretches of slow water pushed Cowden to paddle continuously.

It’s 1,579km down the Ohio to its confluence with the Mississippi in Illinois, which Cowden and Enzo aim to complete in under 40 days. They’re currently on pace, averaging about 20km a day.

Cowden posts regular updates on Facebook and on the expedition’s webpage.

18 Jobs for Retirees – What They Pay and When Social Security Holds Back Benefits

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (359 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that pick retirement work by its pay, its schedule, and how it fits your Social Security claim.
  • In the year you reach full retirement age, 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, Social Security holds back $1 for every $3 you earn above $65,160.
  • Because withheld benefits are credited back at full retirement age, the test is about when to claim, not whether to work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that pick retirement work by its pay, its schedule, and how it fits your Social Security claim. Claim before full retirement age, and until the year you reach it, Social Security holds back $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 a year. Your check rises at that age to account for the months withheld.

In the year you reach full retirement age, 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, Social Security holds back $1 for every $3 you earn above $65,160. It counts only what you earn before the month you reach that age, and from that month on, your earnings no longer reduce your benefit.

Because withheld benefits are credited back at full retirement age, the test is about when to claim, not whether to work. A job that pays well above the limit is a reason to wait to claim, while one that pays less leaves your check untouched.

In a recent development, social Security counts only pay from work toward the limit. That means wages, including bonuses, commissions, and vacation pay, or net profit if you’re self-employed. A pension, an annuity, interest, and investment income don’t count, so a retiree who consults while drawing a pension is tested on the consulting income alone.

To check a job against the limit, multiply its hourly pay by the hours you plan to work. Tutoring 20 hours a week for 50 weeks at the $20.84 median comes to $20,840, under the $24,480 limit.

Before you take a job that will pay more than the limit, enter your expected pay in Social Security’s earnings test calculator to see how much it would hold back.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, open Axos Business Interest Checking for the cash your business keeps on hand to pay bills. Keep a $5,000 average daily balance to skip the $10 monthly fee, and stay under $50,000 to earn its top rate of 1.01%. At $50,000, the whole balance earns 0.20%, so put larger reserves in a business savings account.

Industry observers note that money a business keeps in checking for payroll, rent, and supplier bills has to stay where it can be spent the day a bill comes due. Axos Business Interest Checking pays 1.01% APY, the annual percentage yield, on balances up to $49,999.99, with no minimum number of transactions or card purchases required to earn it. It also charges a $10 monthly fee unless its average daily balance for the month reaches $5,000. Once the balance reaches $50,000, the rate on the whole balance, not just the part above the line, drops to 0.20%.

According to recent reports, axos Bank released online on July 4, 2000, and is headquartered in San Diego, with offices in Las Vegas. It reports more than $28.2 billion in assets, and its parent organization, Axos Financial, trades on the New York Stock Exchange as AX. The Better Business Bureau rates it A+. For small businesses it offers savings and two checking accounts, one that pays interest and one that doesn’t, plus payroll, card processing, and loans backed by the U.S. Small Business Administration through partner companies.

Three things decide whether the account is worth it: how its rate tiers work, what it costs to keep, and how money gets in and out of an online bank.

Axos doesn’t pay each tier’s rate on just the dollars in that tier. Its account agreement applies one daily rate to the balance, and its rate table sets that rate by the range the balance falls in, so a $50,000 balance earns 0.20% on every dollar.

Take the rates Axos posted on November 15, 2026, and a balance that holds steady for a year. A business with $49,999 in the account earns about $505. One with $50,000 earns about $100, and it would take more than $500,000 in the account to earn $505 again.

It has been revealed that the waiver runs on the month’s average, so the balance can dip under $5,000 for a few days around payroll without triggering the fee, as long as the month averages $5,000 or more. A month that falls short costs $10, while $5,000 earns about $4 a month at the rate Axos posted in November 2026.

The 100-item limit counts every debit, credit, and deposited check, so a business that pays many small bills or takes frequent payments can go over it in a busy month.

Checks go in through the Axos app or by mail. Cash goes in at an ATM that takes deposits, using the business debit card. Axos asks customers not to mail cash, and a deposit at an ATM Axos doesn’t own may not be available until the fifth business day after it’s made.

Relying on ATMs for cash makes the account a poor fit for a shop that takes in cash every day. A business paid by card, check, or transfer has little cash to deposit.

Industry observers note that the account pays best on operating cash, the money that has to stay in checking anyway to cover the next month’s payroll, rent, and card bills. Reserves, the money beyond next month’s bills, earn more in Axos Business Premium Savings, which pays 3.50% APY on balances up to $4,999,999.99 against this account’s top rate of 1.01%, with no monthly fee or minimum opening deposit. Savings gives up some access in return, since Axos charges $0.30 for each item past 20 a month and can limit certain savings withdrawals to six a month.

Run the rates Axos posted on November 15, 2026, for a business with $60,000 at Axos, held for a year. Left in Business Interest Checking, the whole $60,000 earns the second tier’s rate, about $120. Kept as $20,000 in checking for bills and $40,000 in Premium Savings, the same money earns about $1,602, with $202 coming from checking and $1,400 from savings.

Industry observers note that axos Basic Business Checking pays no interest, but it reimburses two outgoing domestic wires a month. For a business that sends two, that saves $30 a month, and Interest Checking earns that much only on an average balance above about $35,600 at the November 2026 rate.

Sources indicate that deposits carry FDIC insurance, the federal guarantee on bank deposits, up to the standard $250,000. Every account a business holds at Axos under the same ownership, through any of its brands, counts toward that one limit.

For balances above it, Axos offers Insured Cash Sweep through the IntraFi network, which splits deposits into amounts under $250,000 at other FDIC-insured banks and extends coverage up to $265 million. Axos says swept deposits earn interest but doesn’t publish the rate. The business keeps one relationship and one statement with Axos, a relationship manager sets it up, and the program’s limits and eligibility rules apply.

The account connects to QuickBooks, in its desktop and online versions, and to the desktop version of Quicken, syncing directly or through a file downloaded from Axos.

Support comes from business relationship managers, by phone at 844-678-2726 on weekdays from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Pacific time, and through secure messages in online banking. Axos’s business support pages list no weekend phone hours.

Each business can open one Interest Checking account. Axos opens business accounts only for companies in the United States, and the business and each owner and signer need a physical address on file.

Axos Business Interest Checking is a good place for a business’s bill money and a poor place for its savings. Its strongest case is a business that keeps a steady $5,000 to $50,000 in checking, stays within 100 transactions a month, and rarely wires money out, since that business earns 1.01% on cash that would otherwise sit idle.

It’s the wrong account for a business that deposits cash daily, sends several wires a month, or lets its balance run past $50,000. Keep a month of bills in Interest Checking, below $50,000, and move the rest into Axos Business Premium Savings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Open Axos ONE if your paycheck already arrives by direct deposit. Each month with at least $1,500 in direct deposits and an average checking balance of at least $1,500, savings earns 4.21% APY, and the bundle charges no monthly or overdraft fees. If your deposits vary month to month, pick a savings account that pays its rate without conditions.

Most banks pay little on savings. The national average rate is 0.38% APY, or annual percentage yield, according to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, so a better rate usually means a second bank, away from the checking account your paycheck lands in. Axos ONE pairs checking and high-yield savings at one online bank and ties the savings rate to the checking side. In any month the checking account meets its deposit and balance terms, savings earns the boosted rate. In a month it misses them, savings drops to 1.00% and checking earns nothing.

Sources indicate that axos Bank opened as Bank of Internet USA on July 4, 2000, one of the first banks built to run fully online, and took the Axos name in 2018. It’s based in San Diego, and its parent, Axos Financial, trades on the New York Stock Exchange and reported $30.8 billion in total assets at the end of September 2026. Axos also runs UFB Direct, which matters for the new-customer promotion and the deposit insurance below.

Axos ONE is two accounts opened together, and the checking account’s activity decides the rates on both.

It has been revealed that most of the bundle’s value is in savings. In a qualifying month it pays 4.21% APY on balances up to $249,999.99 and 3.50% on the portion above that. In any other month, the whole balance earns 1.00%.

In a recent development, checking pays 0.51% APY in a qualifying month and nothing otherwise. There’s no monthly fee, no minimum balance, and no overdraft or nonsufficient-funds fee. A payment your balance can’t cover may still be paid or returned, just without a charge. A direct deposit can arrive up to two days early, depending on whether and when your payer funds it. The Visa debit card works fee-free at more than 95,000 ATMs, and Axos reimburses up to $10 a month in other banks’ domestic ATM fees.

The bank’s standalone Axos Checking pays 1.00% APY, a promotional rate, in any statement cycle with at least $1 in direct deposits, and reimburses domestic ATM fees without a cap, but it carries no savings boost. If you only need checking, Axos Checking or another free checking account without a balance requirement is the simpler choice.

Each month, the checking account must meet both halves of one option for either account to earn its boosted rate:.

Industry observers note that both accounts must also be open on the 25th and on the day interest is paid. A fresh account’s first window starts the day it opens, and one opened on or after the 25th starts qualifying the next month.

The fairest yardstick for those terms is Axos’s own Summit Savings, which pays 3.75% APY with no minimum balance and no monthly requirements. Take $20,000 kept in savings for a year at the rates Axos paid when this review was written. At 4.21%, qualifying every month earns about $842 in Axos ONE, $92 more than the $750 Summit Savings pays at 3.75%. At the 1.00% base rate, missing every month earns about $200, $550 less than Summit.

New customers who open the bundle by December 1, 2026 can earn 5.00% APY on up to $49,999.99 of savings for six statement cycles, the opening cycle included, or five when the account opens on or after the 25th. Each cycle still has to meet the monthly terms, and the boost is off in any cycle the savings balance averages $250,000 or more. Anyone who holds or has ever held an Axos Bank or UFB Direct account, loan, or investment is excluded, so opening another Axos account first, Summit Savings included, rules you out. At the rates when this review was written, the boost adds 0.79 percentage points, about $197 over six cycles on a full $49,999.99.

Industry observers note that the fees Axos ONE does charge cover less routine moves. Outgoing wires cost $35 within the U.S. and $45 abroad, incoming wires are free, and debit card purchases and ATM withdrawals in a foreign currency carry a 1% conversion fee.

Axos works online, so the app and the phone carry most of the load. Its Axos All-In-One Mobile Banking app holds a 4.7-star rating from about 20,000 ratings on Apple’s App Store, and a Direct Banker answers the phone 24/7, Thanksgiving and Christmas aside. Checks deposited by phone are held five days.

In a recent development, cash is the awkward part. You can deposit it at participating ATMs or at the register of retailers in the Green Dot network, such as 7-Eleven, CVS, and Walmart. The store may charge up to $4.95 per deposit, and each deposit can run $20 to $500, more at Walmart and ACE Cash Express.

Recent findings suggest that deposits are insured by the FDIC through Axos Bank up to $250,000 per depositor in each ownership category, such as individual or joint. Money you keep at UFB Direct or any other Axos brand counts toward the same limit, since Axos insures them all under one FDIC certificate.

For larger savings, the Axos Insured Deposit Program moves money from Axos ONE Savings to partner banks, each insuring up to the same limit, for up to $2.5 million in additional coverage. Enrolling online or in the app is free and leaves your rate and features unchanged. Checking stays outside the program. You also can’t exclude a partner bank, and Axos leaves it to you to watch which banks hold your money, which matters if you already bank at one of them.

It has been revealed that axos ONE works best as a home for a paycheck that already arrives by direct deposit. That deposit, plus a $1,500 cushion in checking, earns savings the boosted rate, no part of the bundle charges a monthly or overdraft fee, and the extra FDIC coverage is free. For a saver who wants checking and savings at one bank, that’s a strong combination.

Industry observers note that it’s a poor fit for freelancers and others whose deposits arrive irregularly and for anyone who can’t spare $1,500 in checking, since Summit Savings or another account with no monthly terms would earn them more. Savers who move money out often or deposit cash will run into its six-withdrawal limit and paid cash deposits. Readers whose paycheck clears $1,500 a month should open the bundle and point the direct deposit to its checking account so it posts by the 25th.

6 Best Subscription Management Apps (To Cancel Recurring Transactions)

📅 11 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Managing your money isn’t just about earning more.
  • Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.
  • Rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Managing your money isn’t just about earning more. It’s also about stopping unnecessary losses. In today’s digital economy, recurring subscription charges (streaming services, premium apps, trials, memberships) quietly drain money each month. Most people spend hundreds, or even thousands, annually on services they don’t use. Subscription manager apps help you see recurring charges, track billing cycles, and cancel those you no longer want.

Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.

Rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers. It scans your linked bank and credit accounts for recurring charges and displays them on a clear dashboard. People like it for its ability to detect subscriptions and assist with cancellations directly in the app, a major time-saver for busy people.

Why it stands out• Automatically detects recurring payments• Lets you cancel unwanted subscriptions directly from the app• Includes extra budgeting tools and spending alerts• Trusted security with read-only bank access.

Who it’s for: People who want the fastest way to spot and stop unwanted recurring charges without manually entering every service.

Trim is another financial assistant that scans transactions and flags recurring charges. While subscription tracking is a smaller part of its feature set, it also provides bill negotiation support and money-saving alerts. Many owners like Trim because it reaches out on your behalf about subscriptions via text or in-app messaging.

Why it stands out• Recurring transaction detection• Alerts about unusual subscriptions or trials converting to paid• Bill negotiation tools beyond basic subscription tracking.

Who it’s for: Owners who want automation plus help reducing bills and optimizing spending.

Industry observers note that pocketGuard is primarily a budgeting app that includes subscription tracking as part of a broader financial overview. Instead of being solely a subscription manager, it integrates recurring expenses into your overall budget, helping you get a full picture of your finances.

Why it stands out• Syncs automatically with financial accounts• Highlights recurring expenses in the context of your whole budget• Helps track cash flow and affordability.

Who it’s for: People who want subscriptions tracked inside a complete personal finance dashboard.

It has been revealed that monarch Money offers robust financial planning tools: budgets, goals, net worth tracking, and more, with subscription visibility included in the package. Customers often choose it for its highly customizable interface and deep analytics. It’s not subscription-only, but it gives you full clarity on recurring expenses as part of larger planning.

Why it stands out• Powerful budgeting + subscription tracking.• Clean, customizable data visuals.• Goal-based money management.

Who it’s for: Customers who want subscription insights in the context of total financial planning — and who are okay paying for premium features.

If you don’t want to link bank accounts, Bobby is a lightweight subscription tracker that lets you manually enter each subscription, along with billing dates and amounts. It then sends reminders so you don’t forget renewals. It’s simple, privacy-friendly, and great for a hands-on approach.

Why it stands out• No bank/credit card linking required.• Clean and minimal interface.• Calendar views and notification reminders.

Who it’s for: Privacy-focused customers or those who prefer full manual control.

Industry observers note that subby offers functionality similar to Bobby’s but is known for integrations and subscription reminders tailored for Android users. It lets you manually track expenses with flexible billing schedules and alerts. (While not all resources list Subby as a top pick, it’s frequently mentioned among good manual trackers.).

Why it stands out• Manual entry with customizable notifications.• Good choice for Android customers.

Who it’s for: People who want a simple manual tracker without linking financial accounts.

If you’d rather not use a third-party app at all, both Apple and Google offer direct subscription management:.

iPhone (Apple Subscriptions):Settings → Your Name → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel Subscription.

Android (Google Play):Open Google Play → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel subscription.

These built-in tools won’t automatically find all recurring charges if some are billed outside the app stores, but they are a secure and effective way to manage many mobile subscriptions.

Here’s a quick guide based on what matters most to you:.

You can also combine approaches — use a subscription app plus your budgeting system to spot recurring leaks and plan better for annual vs monthly charges.

Subscription manager apps help plug the leaks in your financial bucket, so more of your hard-earned money stays where it belongs: with you. Whether you want automatic detection and help with cancellations, a full financial overview, or full privacy with manual entry, there’s an option that fits your style. Explore one or two subscription manager apps that align with your priorities, and don’t forget to check your finances regularly.

Sources indicate that when I became an accredited investor, I found myself among an elite group with the financial means and regulatory clearance to access investments that many couldn’t. This opened doors to exclusive realms like hedge funds, venture capital firms, specific investment funds, private equity funds, and more.

Even though I had this “exclusive access” it took me a while to start investing in alternative asset classes.

The Securities and Exchange Commission states that as an accredited investor, I possess a level of sophistication that equips me to craft a riskier investment portfolio than a non-accredited investor. While this might not be universally true for everyone, in my case, I had demonstrated the financial resilience to bear more risk (see barbell investing), especially if my investments took an unforeseen downturn.

One of the intriguing aspects I discovered was that investment opportunities for accredited investors aren’t mandated to register with financial authorities. This means they often come with fewer disclosures and might not be as transparent as the registered securities available to the general public.

The underlying belief is that my status as a sophisticated investor implies a deeper understanding of financial risks, a need for less disclosure of unregistered securities, and a conviction that these exclusive investment opportunities are apt for my funds.

It has been revealed that on a personal note, as a practicing CFP®, I haven’t always worked with accredited investors. Early in my career, I didn’t quite grasp the allure. However, as time went on, I began to see the broader spectrum of investment options available to accredited investors.

Sources indicate that as I learned more the clearer it became why this realm was so sought after. The variety and potential of these exclusive opportunities were truly eye-opening, reshaping my perspective on the world of investing.

Sources indicate that an accredited investor is an individual or a business entity that is allowed to trade securities that may not be registered with financial authorities. They are entitled to this privileged access because they satisfy one or more requirements regarding income, net worth, asset size, governance status, or professional experience.

The concept of an accredited investor originated from the idea that individuals or entities with a higher financial acumen or more resources are better equipped to understand and bear the risks of certain investment opportunities.

Historically, the distinction between accredited and non-accredited investors was established to protect less experienced investors from potentially risky or less transparent investment opportunities.

Sources indicate that regulatory bodies, such as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), have set criteria to determine who qualifies as an accredited investor, ensuring that they have the financial stability and sophistication to engage in more complex investment ventures.

To be classified as an accredited investor, one must meet specific criteria set by regulatory bodies:.

The world of accredited investing is dynamic and ever-evolving. Furthermore, technological advancements are playing a pivotal role. The rise of blockchain and tokenized assets, for instance, is creating fresh avenues for investment and might reshape the landscape of opportunities available to accredited investors.

As the line between traditional and alternative investments blurs, the future promises a more integrated, inclusive, and innovative environment for accredited investors.

Typical Promo Biz Class One-Way.

Fuel Surcharges on Promo Awards.

Industry observers note that picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. The couple in economy paid $900 for this flight. You paid 40,000 Flying Blue miles — points you transferred from your Chase Sapphire Reserve in seconds — and the cash value of what you're sitting in is closer to $2,500 to $6,000. That gap is the entire point. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override.

In a recent development, flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

The Fuel Surcharge Nuance You Must Know.

It has been revealed that flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points owners miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

The Transfer Path Is Best-in-Class.

Flying Blue partners with every major transferable currency at a 1:1 ratio:.

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Citi are critical here. When Promo Rewards drop and the best dates start disappearing within hours, you cannot afford a 3-day transfer window. If your points are in Chase or Amex, you can see a seat, transfer, and book in under 10 minutes.

Routing Rules Give You Flexibility.

Sources indicate that flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you plan a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.

Before the 1st of any month arrives, you need to be ready. Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com if you don't have one. More importantly, ensure your transferable points — Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Capital One, or Bilt — are linked and ready. Don't transfer anything yet. You want to see the actual Promo Reward routes before moving a single point.

When the list drops, you'll see a curated set of origin/destination city pairs with fixed Business class prices. Look for transatlantic routes from major U.S. gateways (Upcoming York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Chicago, Miami) to European hubs like Paris (CDG) or Amsterdam (AMS).

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. Enter your origin and destination from the Promo list. Switch the cabin to Business. Search across a 30-day window if possible — the calendar view reveals you which dates have availability. Act within hours, not days. The best dates — particularly weekends, school holidays, and summer dates — disappear fast.

Industry observers note that note: Flying Blue's search only highlights Air France and KLM metal for Promo Rewards. SkyTeam partner availability is separate and won't be Promo-priced.

According to recent reports, do not transfer points yet. Confirm the exact flights, dates, and total miles cost. Take a screenshot. Note the flight numbers and times. Availability can disappear between the moment you see it and the moment you book, so move quickly through the next steps.

From your bank portal (Chase, Amex, Citi), initiate the transfer to Flying Blue. For Chase, Amex, and Citi, transfers are instant. Capital One and Bilt take 1–2 days, so these are less ideal for Promo Rewards' speed-dependent window. Transfer exactly what you need — Promo award prices are fixed, so there's no cushion math required.

In a recent development, with miles in your account, return to the award search, re-confirm your dates are still available, and book. You'll pay the fixed Promo miles price plus taxes and fees (minimal, with no fuel surcharges on Promo awards). You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

According to recent reports, don't panic. Wait for next month. Or search the current month's Promo list for alternative routes — sometimes less popular city pairs have excellent availability. You can also check if the same route appears at standard dynamic pricing, but compare the CPP carefully before transferring for a non-Promo redemption.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic award pricing, which normally makes costs unpredictable and often unfavorable. But the Promo Rewards program creates a monthly fixed-price override on select routes that dramatically undercuts the dynamic system. Each month, Flying Blue publishes a curated list of discounted routes with pricing 25 to 50 percent below standard and with fuel surcharges eliminated entirely. This creates a repeatable, predictable opportunity cycle: check on the 1st, find a discounted route, transfer points instantly from Chase or Amex, and book before the best dates are taken. The structural advantage is that most casual travelers do not know about Promo Rewards or do not act fast enough — which leaves more availability for prepared ChooseFI community members who treat the 1st of each month as a mini-booking event.

Do This: Set a Monthly Calendar Reminder for the 1st.

According to recent reports, flying Blue Promo Rewards are time-sensitive by design. The best routes with the best dates are gone within 24–48 hours of announcement. Put a recurring reminder on your calendar. Treat the 1st of each month like a mini-event.

Do This: Keep a Points Buffer in Your Transferable Accounts.

Because Promo Rewards require fast action and the best transfer partners (Chase, Amex, Citi) are instant, you want at least 40,000–80,000 points already sitting in your transferable account before the announcement. Don't be in a position where you need to wait on a credit card statement to close before you can transfer.

Do This: Use Open-Jaw Routing to Maximize Your Trip.

It has been revealed that flying Blue allows open-jaw routing. Book into Paris (CDG) and out of Amsterdam (AMS) — or any combination of Air France/KLM hub cities — and you've just built a multi-country European trip into a single award booking. This is the kind of routing flexibility that turns a one-city trip into a proper adventure.

Do This: Track Multiple Months of Route Patterns.

Promo routes rotate monthly, but certain routes appear repeatedly — particularly transatlantic and routes between European hubs and Africa or the Middle East. After 2–3 months of observation, you'll start to recognize patterns and can proposal your travel around routes that are likely to repeat.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability.

This is the single biggest mistake beginners make. Always confirm the specific flight, date, and cabin availability before transferring points. Miles are a one-way street — you cannot transfer them back. If availability disappears after you've transferred, you're left with Flying Blue miles that may not be useful for your target route at standard (non-Promo) pricing.

Avoid This: Ignoring Standard Award Pricing.

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing outside of Promo Rewards can be punishingly expensive. A Business class seat that costs 40,000 Promo miles might cost 90,000+ miles at standard dynamic pricing. Always wait for the Promo if you can — patience pays.

The ideal earning setup for this redemption combines a Chase Sapphire Reserve (3x on travel and dining, instant transfer to Flying Blue) with an Amex Gold or Platinum (4x on dining/groceries or 5x on flights respectively, also instant transfer). Between two cards, you can accumulate 40,000–80,000 points in a single year of normal household spending.

Best For: Flexible Couples and Solo Travelers Who Plan in Advance.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI community member who thinks in systems, not spontaneous splurges. You're someone who has already built a transferable points balance of at least 40,000–80,000 points across Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, or Citi ThankYou — and who can act decisively when the right route appears.

In a recent development, couples are the sweet spot. Two people, two Business class seats, one incredible transatlantic experience. Solo travelers benefit enormously too — a single seat at 40,000 miles is one of the highest-CPP solo redemptions in the entire transferable points ecosystem.

Minimum Viable Setup: 40,000 Flying Blue miles or 40,000 transferable points in Chase, Amex, or Citi. A Flying Blue account with verified transfer links. The flexibility to travel within a 30-day window of whatever routes appear that month.

According to recent reports, visit flyingblue.com on the morning of the 1st (or within the first few days) to see the new Promo Rewards routes. Scan for destinations that match your interests. Note the discounted mile pricing and travel date windows — promos typically cover travel within the next 2 to 3 months.

Recent findings suggest that use the Flying Blue award search to check specific dates on the promo routes in business class. Confirm that seats are available at the promo price before you transfer any points. The calendar view lets you scan across multiple dates swiftly.

According to recent reports, transfer the required miles from Chase (instant), Amex (1-2 days), Citi (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Book on flyingblue.com the moment your miles arrive. Do not wait — promo availability is limited and the best dates disappear within hours.

According to recent reports, promo Rewards typically offer 25 to 50 percent off standard dynamic pricing. Amex Membership Rewards and Capital One both transfer at 1:1 but take 1 to 2 business days. Bilt also transfers at 1:1. Since promo availability is time-sensitive, instant transfer partners give you a meaningful speed advantage.

It has been revealed that yes. Promo Rewards rotate destinations each month and cover specific travel date windows, typically 2 to 3 months out. You cannot choose which routes are discounted. The strategy works best for travelers who have a list of destinations they want to visit and can match those against whatever promos appear each month rather than needing a specific route on a specific date.

Sources indicate that the best routes with the best dates typically sell out within 24 to 48 hours of the monthly announcement. Business class availability is particularly limited. Set a reminder for the 1st of each month and check within the first few hours of the announcement for the widest selection of dates and routes.

Industry observers note that this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Recent findings suggest that flying Blue Promo Rewards is the most repeatable sweet spot in travel rewards because it renews every single month. While other sweet spots are one-time plays or annual opportunities, Promo Rewards gives you 12 chances per year to book premium cabin flights at 25 to 50 percent off standard pricing with no fuel surcharges. The system rewards exactly the kind of behavior the FI community already excels at: preparation, patience, and decisive action when the numbers align. Tech Report: U.S. Trio Make First Snowboard and Ski Descent of a Near-7,000'er in Langtang

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).
  • It has been revealed that the team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style.
  • On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

It has been revealed that the team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell.

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

Industry observers note that the expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell mentioned.

Sources indicate that sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell mentioned. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

Industry observers note that after the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram.

“Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell remarked. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

The line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

In a recent development, on the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:.

Industry observers note that the south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

We didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

It took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

In a recent development, A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

Industry observers note that the three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

According to recent reports, “The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

According to recent reports, the hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

In a recent development, “You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”.

It has been revealed that he added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”.

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell noted. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

According to recent reports, childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” said Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell said.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

Recent findings suggest that while this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

It has been revealed that “I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell said. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”.

According to recent reports, “Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Open Axos Basic Business Checking if your business gets paid by card, bank transfer, or wire and you want no monthly fee, no minimum balance, and no cap on transactions.
  • It has been revealed that axos makes a small business choose between earning interest and avoiding fees.
  • It has been revealed that axos has been a digital bank since it opened on July 4, 2000, and runs from its San Diego headquarters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Open Axos Basic Business Checking if your business gets paid by card, bank transfer, or wire and you want no monthly fee, no minimum balance, and no cap on transactions. Skip it if you deposit cash or paper checks often, since both can take until the fifth business day to become available.

It has been revealed that axos makes a small business choose between earning interest and avoiding fees. Its interest-bearing account, Axos Business Interest Checking, charges $10 in any month its average daily balance is under $5,000, plus 50 cents for each transaction past 100 a month. A business that keeps $5,000 there and stays at 100 transactions or fewer earns interest and pays neither fee. Basic Business Checking pays no interest and charges neither fee at any balance or transaction count.

It has been revealed that axos has been a digital bank since it opened on July 4, 2000, and runs from its San Diego headquarters. It counts more than $28.2 billion in assets, and its parent company, Axos Financial, trades on the Upcoming York Stock Exchange as AX. The Better Business Bureau, which has accredited Axos Bank since 2011, rates it A+.

Basic Business Checking’s strength is its short list of fees. Its weakness is getting cash and checks into the account, since Axos has only two branches.

Axos’s account page and its small-business fee schedule, effective September 28, 2026, set these terms:.

Electronic direct deposits are available the day Axos receives them, and incoming wires the next business day. Axos’s account agreement lets it hold other incoming ACH transfers, the standard electronic payments between bank accounts, for up to five business days after they post. The money may be released on the third business day if no payment is returned.

Industry observers note that checks go in through the app, up to 60 a month, $50,000 a business day, and $150,000 in any 30 days. Axos makes them available on the fifth business day after the deposit unless it releases them sooner, so a business paid mostly by check waits about a week for its money.

It has been revealed that cash is harder. In its March 2026 review of the bank, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency counted one branch in San Diego, with an ATM that takes deposits, and one in Las Vegas, which Axos’s agreement says accepts no cash. Elsewhere, cash goes in at other banks’ ATMs that accept deposits, which Axos’s ATM locator finds, and Axos makes it available by the fifth business day at the latest. A business that takes in cash every week should check for one near it before applying.

Recent findings suggest that axos’s app reveals business and personal Axos accounts under one login, moves money between them, and sends wires. Bill Pay comes with the account and usually delivers a payment by ACH in one to three business days, or as a mailed check in up to 10. Its limits are $100,000 for a payment to a organization or a transfer, $10,000 to a person, and $2,500 by email, and Axos won’t raise them.

For bookkeeping, the account connects to QuickBooks Desktop, QuickBooks Online, and Quicken’s desktop version, either directly or through transaction files you download in CSV, QBO, QFX, or OFX format and import.

Industry observers note that A growing business may outgrow the standard platform in two ways. It can’t yet add a user who isn’t a signer on the account, such as a bookkeeper or accountant, and it doesn’t send batches of ACH payments to staff or vendors. Both come with Axos’s treasury management service, its package of payment and fraud-control tools for businesses, which is free for a first account and charges $1 a batch and $1 for each ACH payment past 15 a month.

Industry observers note that axos Bank’s deposits carry Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) coverage up to $250,000 per depositor in each ownership category, the FDIC’s groups for how money is owned, under FDIC certificate 35546. A business that keeps more can ask a relationship manager to set up Axos’s Insured Cash Sweep, which places money at other banks in the IntraFi network and can raise coverage to $265 million, with interest paid on what’s swept.

Sole proprietors should add up their personal money too. The FDIC insures a sole proprietorship’s deposits as the owner’s own, combined with the owner’s other individual accounts at the same bank, and Axos’s UFB Direct brand counts as the same bank. A corporation’s or partnership’s deposits are insured in their own category.

Recent findings suggest that A business formed less than a year before it applies can earn up to $200 by applying with promo code START200 by January 31, 2027. Axos pays $50 for each statement cycle in which the account’s average daily balance is at least $3,000, in any four of its first five statement cycles, counting the month it opens.

The business must also never have been the primary owner of an Axos small-business account, and Axos closes the account if it isn’t approved and funded within 60 days. An account closed within 180 days can be charged up to $200 for closing early, and the bonus may be taxable and reported on a Form 1099.

Sources indicate that the balance costs little to hold. At a sample savings rate of 3.50% annual percentage yield (APY), $3,000 would earn about $35 in four months, by our math. A business that can spare the balance gives up that $35 to collect up to $200.

Sources indicate that an established business can’t use START200, and Axos’s other cash offer needs a large savings balance. A business that pairs the account with Business Premium Savings, opening both in one application with code SBB600 by January 31, 2027, can earn up to $600. Axos pays $100 for each statement cycle in which the business meets four requirements by the 25th of the month. They are a $50,000 average daily balance in savings, a $1,500 average in checking, a deposit of $1,000 or more by ACH, wire, or check from outside Axos, and two debit card purchases of $50 or more.

Industry observers note that business Premium Savings pays 3.50% APY on balances under $5 million with no monthly fee, though it charges 30 cents for each transaction past 20 a month. Only one Axos offer applies to a business at a time.

Axos notes its application takes minutes online. It opens accounts only for businesses in the United States, and every signer must live in the U.S., with a physical address there and a Social Security number, though citizenship isn’t required. The application asks for the business’s Employer Identification Number (EIN), a Social Security number for a sole proprietor, ownership agreements, a business license, and articles of incorporation or organization.

Sources indicate that axos may turn down businesses in industries it restricts, such as cannabis, cryptocurrency, internet gambling, or money services. It also can’t process an application while a freeze is in place at ChexSystems, a firm that reports on checking account history, and it asks applicants to lift any TransUnion credit freeze first.

Recent findings suggest that help comes through one number, 844-678-2726. Relationship managers answer weekdays from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Pacific time, and after hours, on weekends, and on holidays the line handles fraud alerts, card services, and urgent problems. The Visa debit card and any checks ordered with the application arrive in seven to 10 business days.

Sources indicate that axos Basic Business Checking costs close to nothing to run. It has no monthly fee, minimum, or transaction cap, it refunds other banks’ ATM fees, and it covers two outgoing wires a month, so a business paid by card, bank transfer, or wire pays little beyond overdrafts and extra wires.

Sources indicate that A business that handles cash or paper checks every week will wait on its money, since both can take until the fifth business day to become available, and would do better at a bank with a branch nearby. One that keeps a large balance earns nothing here, where Axos’s Business Interest Checking or Business Premium Savings would pay interest. Freelancers and online businesses paid electronically should open it. A business formed within the past year should apply with code START200 by January 31, 2027, and keep $3,000 in it for four of its first five statement cycles to collect the full $200.

#9341. How to Navigate the Tariff Circus
